tasks.title: Introduction
tasks.overview: Python is a language for giving clear instructions to a computer. In this first task, you will see what Python is, where it is used, and what a tiny program looks like.

lesson.heading: What is Python?
lesson.body: Python is a programming language. You write instructions in Python, and the computer follows them in order.

lesson.heading: Where is it used?
lesson.body: People use Python to automate repetitive work, build websites, explore data, create tools, and control devices.

lesson.heading: Your first instruction
lesson.body: print(...) asks Python to display a value. Text needs matching quotation marks inside the parentheses.

lesson.heading: Remember
lesson.body: A program is a set of instructions. Python runs them in order, and print(...) displays a message.

examples.title: Display a welcome
examples.explanation: The text is inside quotes, and print displays it.

project.title: A tiny welcome sign
project.scenario: A friend is setting up a welcome screen for a small study group. They need Python to show a friendly title and a second line that says the group is ready.
project.friendPrompt: Hey {name}, I’m putting together a welcome screen for our study group. How can I make Python show a friendly title and then a second line saying we’re ready?
steps: Add another print instruction underneath it.
Run the program and check both lines appear.

tasks.title: Get Started
tasks.overview: A Python program is a set of instructions saved in a file and run by Python. You will learn the basic run cycle and see why output is useful while building a program.

lesson.heading: Write and run
lesson.body: You can write Python in an editor, save the file with a .py ending, and ask Python to run it.

lesson.heading: Read the output
lesson.body: Output is what the program displays. Compare it with what you expected to spot mistakes early.

lesson.heading: Follow the order
lesson.body: Python begins at the first instruction and continues downward. Each print instruction displays its own line.

lesson.heading: Remember
lesson.body: Save your instructions, run the program, and read the output to check what happened.

examples.title: Two lines of output
examples.explanation: Python runs the first print before the second one.

practicals.prompt: What does a .py file usually contain?
In a few words, what should you check after running a program?
Display Start on one line and Finished on the next.

steps: Display the meeting time on a separate line.
Run it and check the order.

tasks.title: Syntax
tasks.overview: Syntax is the set of rules for writing Python instructions. Matching quotes, parentheses, colons, and indentation help Python understand what you mean.

lesson.heading: Small rules matter
lesson.body: Python expects symbols and words to be in the right order. A missing quote or parenthesis can stop a line from running.

lesson.heading: Match pairs
lesson.body: When you open parentheses or quotes, close them. For example, print("Hello") has matching parentheses and quotation marks.

lesson.heading: Use clear lines
lesson.body: Put separate instructions on separate lines. Later, indentation will show which instructions belong inside a block.

lesson.heading: Remember
lesson.body: Syntax is how code is written. Read the exact error line and check its paired symbols first.

examples.explanation: The opening parenthesis and quote each have a matching close.
